analysis.evidence: Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai, each introduced by the direct-object marker אֶת. The following clause says they set out from Ur for Canaan, showing that Terah took his relatives with him on the journey.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks the Qal wayyiqtol. The verb is third person masculine singular, agreeing with its subject תֶּרַח.
analysis.sense: take a person for relocation

analysis.evidence: וַיִּקַּח תֶּרַח אֶת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ reads “Terah took Abram his son.” The object marker אֶת introduces Abram, and בְּנוֹ identifies him as Terah’s son.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name with no prefix or suffix. It is the subject of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.”
analysis.sense: The father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

analysis.evidence: תֶּרַח is the subject of וַיִּקַּח (“took”). אֶת introduces אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ (“Abram his son”), the first of the people Terah took.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: (marks the definite object)

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of וַיִּקַּח. In אֶת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ, “Abram his son,” בְּנוֹ identifies Abram as Terah’s son. Haqor links the name to אבה through its אָב, “father,” element.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The separate particle אֶת marks Abram as a direct object of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.”
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

draft.change: Add Genesis 11:31 as evidence for the existing definite-object sense of the Hebrew particle.
draft.definition: Introduces the particular person or thing a verb acts on, ordinarily a definite noun identified by the article, a name or a possessive suffix.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 11:31, וְאֶת לוֹט adds Lot to Abram as an object of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.”

analysis.evidence: Terah is the subject of וַיִּקַּח, “took.” After אֶת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ, “Abram his son,” וְאֶת לוֹט adds Lot as the second person Terah took. וְאֵת שָׂרַי continues the same list.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ means “and.” It prefixes the unsuffixed direct-object particle אֶת, a form of אֵת.
analysis.sense: Marks Lot as a definite direct object.

evidence.note: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Terah’s genealogy names Lot as Haran’s son and Abram’s nephew. The passage gives no explanation of the name.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט with its etymology unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Lot as the son whom Haran fathered.

analysis.evidence: In וְאֶת לוֹט בֶּן הָרָן, the separate object marker introduces Lot as one of the people Terah took, and בֶּן הָרָן identifies him as Haran’s son.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Haran’s son.

analysis.evidence: לוֹט בֶּן הָרָן means “Lot, son of Haran.” The marked בֶּן identifies Haran as Lot’s father.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state before the name הָרָן, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: son, male child

evidence.note: After listing Haran among Terah’s sons, the genealogy says וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת לוֹט, “and Haran fathered Lot.”

article.name: הָרָן
article.summary: Genesis 11:27 names Haran alongside Abram and Nahor as a son of Terah. It then identifies him as the father of Lot.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for הָרָן with the etymology left open.
draft.definition: Haran, the personal name borne here by Terah’s son and Lot’s father.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 identifies Haran through both family relationships. The verse gives no derivation for his name.

analysis.evidence: לוֹט בֶּן הָרָן identifies Lot as Haran’s son. The following בֶּן בְּנוֹ, “his son’s son,” identifies Lot as Terah’s grandson through Haran. The verse gives no derivation for the name.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The initial ה belongs to the name. The word has no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Haran, son of Terah and father of Lot

analysis.evidence: In בֶּן בְּנוֹ, “son of his son,” the marked בֶּן identifies Lot as the son of Haran. The following בְּנוֹ identifies Haran as Terah’s son, so the whole phrase describes Lot as Terah’s grandson.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: son, male child

evidence.note: The verse explicitly gives Sarai as the name of Abram’s wife.
God identifies שָׂרַי as Abraham’s wife and gives her the name שָׂרָה.
Kings and their noblewomen appear in parallel. The noun for the women, שָׂרוֹת, is the plural of שָׂרָה.

article.name: שָׂרַי
article.summary: Sarai is the name by which Abram’s wife is introduced. Her later name שָׂרָה has the same form as the Hebrew noun for a princess or noblewoman, supporting a similar meaning for Sarai. The text leaves the force of the earlier name’s ending unexplained.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for שָׂרַי linked to the שׂרר word family.
draft.definition: Sarai, the earlier name of Abram’s wife Sarah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:29 names Abram’s wife Sarai. Genesis 17:15 gives both names when God tells Abraham to call her Sarah.

analysis.evidence: וְאֵת marks שָׂרַי as another person Terah took with him. The following phrases כַּלָּתוֹ and אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם identify Sarai as Terah’s daughter-in-law and Abram’s wife.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The final י is part of the name.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abram’s wife before she was named Sarah.

analysis.evidence: The phrase אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ identifies Sarai as the wife of Terah’s son Abram, establishing her relationship to Terah.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Terah.
analysis.sense: daughter-in-law

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68381:6, 68381:10.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state. The following name אַבְרָם identifies whose wife she is.
analysis.sense: wife

draft.change: Clear the unsupported root אבה and its link to article 2bh. Preserve the explanation of the compound name and its recorded bearer.
draft.definition: Abram, the earlier name of Abraham, son of Terah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:26 identifies Abram as Terah’s son, and Genesis 17:5 records his change of name. The first element of אַבְרָם is the noun אָב, “father.” Neither verse supports deriving the name from אָבָה, “be willing.”

analysis.evidence: The phrase אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ means “the wife of Abram his son.” It identifies Sarai as Abram’s wife and Abram as Terah’s son.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name with no prefix or suffix. It follows the construct noun אֵשֶׁת and names Sarai’s husband.
analysis.sense: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham

draft.change: Add Genesis 11:31 as an example of ben-son for בֵּן at word index 0 in bnh.
draft.definition: A male child in relation to his parent.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:31 calls Sarai the wife of Abram and identifies Abram as Terah’s son.

analysis.evidence: In אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ, “the wife of Abram his son,” בְּנוֹ identifies Abram as Terah’s son. The verse has already called Abram אַבְרָם בְּנוֹ, and it identifies Sarai as Terah’s daughter-in-law.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct of the common noun בֵּן with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix וֹ. The suffix refers to Terah.
analysis.sense: son, male child

analysis.evidence: מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים names their point of departure, Ur of the Chaldeans, and לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן gives their intended destination, Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks the Qal wayyiqtol. The ending וּ marks the third-person masculine plural form.
analysis.sense: go out, depart from a place or someone’s presence

analysis.evidence: With וַיֵּצְאוּ (“they set out”), מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים identifies Ur of the Chaldeans as the place Terah and his family left on their way to Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מֵ־, a form of מִן meaning “from,” precedes the proper noun אוּר.
analysis.sense: Ur of the Chaldeans

draft.change: Add Genesis 11:31 as an example of the existing gentilic sense.
draft.definition: A member of the Chaldean people. The plural can designate the people collectively.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:31 repeats the designation אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים found in Genesis 11:28.

analysis.evidence: In מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים, “from Ur of the Chaldeans,” the plural names the people associated with Ur. The whole phrase identifies the travelers’ point of departure.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. This is the masculine plural absolute of the gentilic כַּשְׂדִּי. The initial כ belongs to the stem.
analysis.sense: a member of the Chaldean people

analysis.evidence: וַיֵּצְאוּ describes their departure from Ur of the Chaldeans. לָלֶכֶת gives their purpose, and אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן names their intended destination, the land of Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לָ introduces the Qal infinitive construct לֶכֶת and marks the purpose of their departure.
analysis.sense: go, move from place to place

analysis.evidence: In לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן, “to go to the land of Canaan,” כְּנַעַן names the territory toward which Terah’s party set out.
analysis.morphology: Common noun of both genders, singular construct before כְּנַעַן, with directional ה marking the goal of motion.
analysis.sense: land, country, territory

analysis.evidence: לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן means “to go to the land of Canaan.” כְּנַעַן names the land the travelers intended to reach.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אַרְצָה carries the directional ending ־ָה.
analysis.sense: the land of Canaan

analysis.evidence: עַד חָרָן gives the extent of their journey: they came as far as Haran. וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם then says they settled there.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol. The ending וּ marks the third-person masculine plural.
analysis.sense: come, arrive

analysis.evidence: In וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד חָרָן, “they came as far as Haran,” עַד marks the place the travelers reached. וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם, “they settled there,” confirms that they stopped at Haran.
analysis.morphology: Simple Hebrew preposition with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: as far as, up to, to (a place or person)

draft.change: Add Genesis 11:32 as an example of the existing haran sense.
draft.definition: Haran, the place where Terah and his household settled on their journey from Ur toward Canaan.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:32 identifies Haran as the place of Terah’s death.

analysis.evidence: וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד חָרָן means “they came as far as Haran.” The following שָׁם (“there”) refers back to Haran as the place where they settled. Lot’s father, הָרָן, is spelled with initial ה earlier in the verse.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding preposition עַד is a separate word.
analysis.sense: Haran, the place where Terah settled and died.

analysis.evidence: The party set out for Canaan but reached Haran. After וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד חָרָן, “they came as far as Haran,” שָׁם points back to Haran as the place where they settled.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks the Qal wayyiqtol. The verb is third-person masculine plural, with Terah and his party as its subject.
analysis.sense: to take up residence in a place

analysis.evidence: וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד חָרָן says they reached Haran. In וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם, “they settled there,” שָׁם refers back to Haran.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew adverb of place with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: At the place just mentioned.
